question: Real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) are chosen with \(1 \lt a \lt b\) such that no triangle with positive area has side lengths \(1,\) \(a,\) and \(b\) or \(\tfrac1b,\) \(\tfrac1a,\) and \(1.\) What is the smallest possible value of \(b?\)
solution:
For three positive lengths in increasing order, a triangle has positive area exactly when the two smaller lengths sum to more than the largest. Here \(1<a<b\), so the first proposed triangle fails exactly when
\[
1+a\le b,
\]
or \(a\le b-1\). In particular, \(b>2\).

The reciprocal lengths satisfy \(1/b<1/a<1\). Thus the second proposed triangle fails exactly when
\[
\frac1b+\frac1a\le1.
\]
Because \(a\), \(b\), and \(b-1\) are positive, we may multiply and divide by them without changing the inequality direction. The reciprocal condition becomes
\[
a+b\le ab,
\qquad a(b-1)\ge b,
\qquad a\ge\frac{b}{b-1}.
\]
The lower and upper bounds on \(a\) must be compatible, so
\[
\frac{b}{b-1}\le b-1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b^2-3b+1\ge0.
\]
The roots of \(b^2-3b+1=0\) are
\[
\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2},\qquad \frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
The quadratic is nonnegative outside the interval between these roots. Since \(b>2\), only the upper range is possible:
\[
b\ge\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
To check attainment, take \(a=(1+\sqrt5)/2\) and \(b=a+1=(3+\sqrt5)/2\). These satisfy \(1<a<b\) and \(a^2=a+1\). Consequently,
\[
ab=a^2+a=2a+1=a+b,
\]
so \(1/a+1/b=1\), while \(1+a=b\). Both triples are degenerate and therefore have no positive area, as required. The smallest possible value is \(\boxed{\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
